content: Despite significant evidence highlighting the long-term consequences of unrelieved pain during infancy, pain management in this population remains insufficiently addressed. Inadequate pain management during this critical period of rapid development can have lifelong implications. A systematic and comprehensive review of pain management strategies is essential to ensure appropriate care for infants experiencing procedural pain. This review serves as an update to a previously published Cochrane review from 2015. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and potential adverse effects of non-pharmacological interventions for managing acute procedural pain in infants and young children up to three years of age. Interventions such as kangaroo care, sucrose, breastfeeding, breast milk, and music were excluded from this analysis. The review incorporated data from 138 studies, including 76 new studies, with a total of 11,058 participants. Of these, 115 studies (9,048 participants) were included in the quantitative analysis, while 23 studies (2,010 participants) were described qualitatively due to limitations in statistical reporting or being the sole study in their category. The review assessed pain responses during two distinct phases: pain reactivity (within the first 30 seconds following a painful stimulus) and immediate pain regulation (after the first 30 seconds). The level of certainty in the evidence was evaluated using the Cochrane risk of bias tool and the GRADE approach. Effect sizes were determined using the standardised mean difference (SMD), with thresholds defined as small (0.2), moderate (0.5), and large (0.8) effects. Heterogeneity was also assessed, with thresholds ranging from not important (0%-40%) to considerable (75%-100%). The most commonly studied procedures were heel sticks (63 studies) and needlestick procedures for vaccinations or vitamin administration (35 studies). A significant proportion of the studies (103 out of 138) were judged to have a high risk of bias, primarily due to issues with blinding of personnel and outcome assessors. In preterm neonates, non-nutritive sucking demonstrated a moderate reduction in pain reactivity (SMD -0.57, 95% CI -1.03 to -0.11) and a moderate improvement in immediate pain regulation (SMD -0.61, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.27), although the evidence was of very low certainty. Facilitated tucking showed a large reduction in pain reactivity (SMD -1.01, 95% CI -1.44 to -0.58) and a moderate improvement in immediate pain regulation (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -0.92 to -0.26), also based on very low-certainty evidence. Swaddling did not significantly reduce pain reactivity (SMD -0.60, 95% CI -1.23 to 0.04) but showed a large improvement in immediate pain regulation (SMD -1.21, 95% CI -2.05 to -0.38), again with very low-certainty evidence. In full-term neonates, non-nutritive sucking was associated with a large reduction in pain reactivity (SMD -1.13, 95% CI -1.57 to -0.68) and a large improvement in immediate pain regulation (SMD -1.49, 95% CI -2.20 to -0.78), based on very low-certainty evidence. For older full-term infants, structured parental involvement was the most studied intervention. However, it showed little to no effect on reducing pain reactivity (SMD -0.18, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.03) or improving immediate pain regulation (SMD -0.09, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.21), with lowto moderate-certainty evidence. Adverse events were rarely reported, with only two studies documenting such events. These included vomiting in one preterm neonate and oxygen desaturation in one full-term neonate in the NICU following non-nutritive sucking. The findings of this review were limited by considerable heterogeneity in the data and the predominance of very lowto low-certainty evidence. Non-nutritive sucking, facilitated tucking, and swaddling may reduce pain behaviors in preterm neonates, while non-nutritive sucking may also be effective in full-term neonates. However, no interventions demonstrated strong evidence for reducing pain behaviors in older infants. Further high-quality research is necessary to draw definitive conclusions and improve confidence in these findings.
